what_its_for: Fluocinolone acetonide is a corticosteroid (steroid) medicine used to reduce redness, swelling, and itching caused by skin conditions like eczema, psoriasis, rashes, and allergic reactions. Some forms are used to treat inflammation in the ear or eye.
how_to_take: For skin (cream, ointment, or solution): Wash your hands before and after applying. Clean and dry the affected area. Apply a thin layer to the skin and gently rub it in. Do not cover the area with a bandage or wrap unless your doctor tells you to. For ear drops: Lie on your side or tilt your head so the affected ear faces up. Gently pull the ear back and drop the medicine in. Stay in that position for a few minutes. For the eye implant: This is placed in your eye by your doctor in a clinic or operating room — you do not put it in yourself.
dosing: The dose depends on the form you are using and what condition is being treated. For skin creams or ointments: usually applied 2 to 4 times a day, or as directed by your doctor. For ear drops: usually 5 drops in the affected ear twice a day for 2 weeks. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and do not use more or less than prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, apply or use it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not double up on doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not freeze the cream, ointment, or ear drops. Keep the cap tightly closed when not in use. Keep all forms of this medicine out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Do not use this medicine near your eyes, inside your nose, or inside your mouth unless it is specifically made for that area. Do not use on broken, infected, or wounded skin unless directed by your doctor. Avoid getting the skin form in contact with your eyes. Do not wear tight bandages or plastic wrap over the treated skin unless your doctor tells you to, as this can increase the amount of medicine absorbed into your body. Avoid using this medicine longer than recommended, as overuse can thin the skin or cause other side effects.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor if you notice: skin thinning, stretch marks, or bruising easily in the treated area; signs of skin infection such as increased redness, warmth, pus, or worsening pain; your condition does not improve or gets worse after a few weeks of treatment; you have unusual weight gain, a round or puffy face, increased thirst or urination, or extreme tiredness (these could be signs your body is absorbing too much steroid); vision changes if you are using the eye form; or any severe allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: Most people notice some improvement in redness and itching within a few days of starting treatment. Full improvement may take 1 to 2 weeks depending on your condition. If you do not see improvement after 2 weeks, contact your doctor.
special_populations: Children: Use with caution in children because their skin absorbs more medicine, which can increase the risk of side effects. Use the lowest dose possible for the shortest time needed. Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Talk to your doctor before using this medicine. It should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. If breastfeeding, avoid applying it to the chest or breast area. Elderly patients: Older adults may have thinner skin and are more sensitive to side effects. Use only as directed by your doctor.
